h2: Heat exchanger inspection services: what a full bundle scope covers
html:
Searches for heat exchanger inspection services usually come from a turnaround planner or a reliability engineer who has a bundle coming out and needs more than a tube count. Tube testing is the largest part of the job, but a useful heat exchanger inspection also covers the shell, the channel and the tubesheet, and it ends with a plugging list and a tube map the owner's engineer can act on.

Tube-side methods, chosen by tube material

Non-ferrous tubes (copper alloys, stainless steel, titanium) are tested with bobbin-coil eddy current testing, the fastest way to find wall loss, pitting and cracking along the full length of every tube. Carbon steel and other ferromagnetic tubes need remote field testing (RFT) for screening, or near-field testing on finned air-cooler tubes. Where a measured remaining wall matters more than speed, IRIS tube inspection (rotating ultrasonic) measures the wall directly and is the usual prove-up for RFT calls. Most programmes combine them: electromagnetic screening of the whole bundle, then IRIS on a sample and on every tube with a significant indication.

Shell, channel, nozzles and tubesheet

The pressure boundary outside the tubes is a pressure vessel and is inspected like one, under the owner's API 510 programme and API RP 572: UT thickness at the condition monitoring locations on the shell and channel, corrosion mapping where pitting or flow-assisted wall loss is expected, MT or PT on nozzle and attachment welds, and visual examination of the tubesheet face, gasket surfaces and baffles once the bundle is pulled. Tube-to-tubesheet joints and ligaments are examined visually, with PT where the service calls for it.

What heat exchanger testing needs from the plant

Results are only as good as the cleaning. Tubes must be cleaned to bare metal and the tube ends must be accessible. The plant should send the tube material, diameter and wall gauge, the tube layout drawing and the last inspection report, so the calibration standards match the tubes and this outage's readings can be compared with the last ones. Heat exchanger testing in the pressure sense, a shell-side or tube-side hydrostatic or leak test, is normally run by the maintenance contractor; the NDE shows where a tube leaks, why, and how much wall is left in its neighbours.

What you receive

A heat exchanger tube inspection report should carry the procedure and the calibration standard used, the technician's certification level, a tubesheet map, a list of every tube with an indication sized by depth band, the tubes recommended for plugging against the owner's criteria, and photographs of the tubesheet and shell. Plugging and retubing decisions belong to the owner's engineer; the report gives them the evidence. References include ASME Section V Article 8, ASTM E690 for in-situ eddy current examination of non-magnetic tubes and ASTM E2096 for remote field testing of ferromagnetic tubes.

United States and Canada

In the US an exchanger is usually inspected under the owner's API 510 programme and, at covered facilities, OSHA process safety management. In Canada its design carries a provincial registration (CRN) and the provincial regulator, such as ABSA in Alberta or TSSA in Ontario, sets the in-service rules, with intervals set inside an approved owner-user programme where the plant has one. Atlantis NDT carries out the NDE and the Level III review, and your Authorized Inspector remains inspector of record. Fired heater coils follow API RP 573 instead; see the fired heater tube inspection guide. For a planned outage, turnaround inspection services explains how the NDE crew fits the schedule, or send us the exchanger list for a scope and quotation.
